text.p: Key commodities including copper, gold, wheat and oil closed lower in overnight trading, pushing the CRB index 1.13 points lower to 234.02.
Copper was subdued and rangebound in the afternoon trading session on Wednesday while other base metals on the London Metal Exchange proved more erratic.
Three months copper ended at $2,267 per tonne, off $11 from Tuesday's close but up sharply from a $2,247 early low.
The metal found good support around $2,250 after tumbling in the pre-market following a sizeable 17,025-tonne rise in LME stocks -- the market's most distinctive feature.
"Copper was confined to the mid-$2,260s in the afternoon, digesting movements of the past few days. It was also overshadowed by action in the other metals," a trader said.
The cash to three months backwardation shrank to $185/$195 from $200 in the morning and a high of $270 on Tuesday.

The stock rise played a big part in taming the backwardation and inventory movements over the next few days would be watched very closely, with many traders saying they expected more increases in coming days.
Aluminium found a late surge of energy in the afternoon and zoomed up to close $7 firmer at $1,570, after initially coming lower with copper in early trading.

Zinc prices was also buoyant, at one point during the afternoon rings re-hurdling the key $1,500 level initially attained on Monday. But it was sold back down again and prices finished just $3 firmer at $1,494.
Tin and nickel, blasted by fund liquidation and stop-loss selling earlier in the day, finished near lows.
Tin crumbled through recent support around $5,500 and dropped to a nadir of $5,430, making a fresh 2-1/3 year low.
It ended just above that at $5,450, a $65 decline.
Nickel also sank, to $6,720 - the lowest level since January 10 - after a midday selling binge. It barely recovered from the lows by the end of the kerb, wrapping up $125 lower at $6,750.

Lead was $6 lower at $632, following steep losses earlier this week from Monday's high of $674.50. It may have done enough on the downside for now, analysts said, but it remained vulnerable to downside pressure as long as it was below $650.

COMEX gold and silver futures saw another intraday rally fade away into a lower close Wednesday, with silver the focus of attack from funds, but platinum group metals (PGMs) managed to end higher. "Silver in particular now looks like its heading south for the summer," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.

"September silver broke down out of the range of the past week, under pressure from selling by funds and locals at the close, but gold did not follow to the same extent as it had already been sold off heavily last week," he said.

COMEX September silver ended down 11.2 cents at $4.185 an ounce, breaking down out of its $4.40-4.24 range of the past week, though it ended just above the contract's lows at $4.175. Volume was only moderate though at 13,000 lots.
In the bullion market, spot silver ended quoted $4.21/23 an ounce, its lowest levels since November 1993.

Meanwhile, COMEX August gold ended down 30 cents at $318.70 an ounce, testing the bottom of its range of the past week, with the August/December spread narrowing further to 3.3 cents. Estimated COMEX gold volume was a healthy 42,000 lots.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $317.80/30, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $319.50 and the New York close Tuesday around $318.50/00.

Gold fixed at a 12 year low last week at $315.75 in London, in the wake of news of a sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Reserve Bank of Australia. "The market is still bearish on gold, as there's still little incentive for investors, given potential central bank and producer selling, and given that overall commodity markets still have an disinflationary tone," Paine Webber analyst Bernard Savaiko said.

Crude prices were unable to shake the prospect of Iraqi oil exports restarting while heating oil absorbed a larger-than-expected stock rise in the API data. API data showed distillate stocks, comprised of heating oil and diesel, rising a surprising 5.5 million barrels when traders forecasted a rise of one to three million barrels. August crude ended off two cents at $19.65 a barrel while August heating oil finished 0.27 cent a gallon lower at 52.68 cents.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed lower on a drop in corn and soybean futures. Forecasts for showers this weekend in key U.S. corn and soybean growing states hit those markets, and wheat fell in sympathy. Wheat also continued to labor under the weight of reports of a bumper harvest this year in the U.S. winter wheat growing region. Wheat closed two to seven cents per bushel lower, with July down seven at $3.25 and September down 6-3/4 at $3.31-1/2.

CSCE world sugar futures closed at two week highs on Wednesday amid brisk chart-driven fund buying. The benchmark October contract rose to 11.34 cents, its highest level since reaching 11.40 cents on July 1, while several of the back months surged to new life-of-contract highs. The October contract closed at 11.30 cents.
